params.question: A trauma patient's chest radiograph is labelled 'AP supine' and shows a cardiothoracic ratio of 0.55. What is the correct interpretation?

answers.text: The patient has cardiomegaly and requires urgent echocardiography

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: On an antero-posterior or supine film, the heart sits farther from the detector and is geometrically magnified. A ratio exceeding 0.5 on such a film is a projection artefact, not reliable evidence of cardiomegaly.

answers.text: The apparent cardiac enlargement is likely a projection artefact; a postero-anterior erect film is needed before assessing heart size

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. On a PA erect film the heart lies close to the detector, minimising magnification. The cardiothoracic ratio threshold of less than 0.5 is valid only on that projection. AP and supine films magnify the heart, making a PA film essential before diagnosing cardiomegaly.

answers.text: A cardiothoracic ratio above 0.5 confirms cardiomegaly regardless of the projection used

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The cardiothoracic ratio threshold applies only to a postero-anterior erect film. AP and supine projections magnify the cardiac silhouette due to geometric beam divergence, producing falsely elevated ratios.

answers.text: The supine position compresses the heart, so the ratio underestimates true heart size

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The opposite is true. A supine or AP film positions the heart farther from the detector, causing magnification. The ratio overestimates heart size on these projections, not underestimates it.

overallFeedback.feedback: On an AP or supine film the heart sits farther from the detector, causing magnification. The cardiothoracic ratio of less than 0.5 applies only to a PA erect radiograph — never diagnose cardiomegaly without confirming projection.
Well done. The cardiothoracic ratio is reliable only on a PA erect film. AP and supine projections magnify the heart due to geometric divergence of the X-ray beam.

interactions.label: A radiograph of a child's wrist shows a radiolucent line between the metaphysis

params.question: A radiograph of a child's wrist shows a radiolucent line between the metaphysis and the epiphysis of the distal radius. What is the most reliable method to distinguish a normal growth plate from a fracture?

answers.text: Order a computed tomography scan of the wrist for detailed bone assessment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CT is unnecessary as the initial step. The simplest and most reliable method is to image the contralateral limb — growth plates are bilaterally symmetrical, whereas fractures are not.

answers.text: Image the contralateral limb and compare for symmetry

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The physis is cartilaginous and therefore radiolucent, producing a lucent line that mimics a fracture. Imaging the opposite limb reveals whether the appearance is symmetrical — growth plates match bilaterally, while fractures do not.

answers.text: Repeat the radiograph after one week to look for callus formation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Waiting one week delays diagnosis and risks complications. The key step is imaging the contralateral limb — bilateral symmetry confirms a normal growth plate, while asymmetry suggests a fracture.

answers.text: Measure the width of the radiolucent line, as growth plates are always wider than fracture lines

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Width alone does not reliably distinguish a growth plate from a fracture. The definitive feature is bilateral symmetry — compare with the opposite limb.

overallFeedback.feedback: The growth plate (physis) is cartilage and appears as a radiolucent line, mimicking a fracture. The reliable distinction is symmetry: image the contralateral limb. Growth plates are symmetrical; fractures are not.
Exactly right. The symmetry test is the key to distinguishing a normal growth plate from a fracture — bilateral symmetry confirms normal anatomy.

params.question: A hand and wrist radiograph taken for age estimation shows that all carpal and phalangeal epiphyses have fused. Which skeletal site is most useful for further age discrimination?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The distal femoral epiphysis fuses by late adolescence and would already be fused at this stage. The medial end of the clavicle — the last bone to fuse, well into the mid-twenties — is the most useful late marker.

Correct. The medial clavicular epiphysis is the last growth plate in the body to fuse, completing well into the mid-twenties. This makes it the definitive marker for distinguishing a late adolescent from an adult when hand-wrist atlas methods can no longer discriminate.

The proximal tibial epiphysis typically fuses in the mid- to late teens. By the time all hand-wrist centres have fused, it is no longer informative. The medial clavicular epiphysis, fusing last of all skeletal sites, is the correct choice.
The greater trochanter fuses in the mid- to late teens and offers no further discriminating value at this stage. The medial end of the clavicle remains open into the mid-twenties.

overallFeedback.feedback: Once all hand-wrist epiphyses have fused, atlas methods like Greulich-Pyle can no longer discriminate. The medial end of the clavicle — the last bone to fuse, well into the mid-twenties — becomes the key marker for age estimation.
Correct. The medial clavicular epiphysis fuses last of all skeletal sites, making it indispensable when hand-wrist atlas methods have lost their discriminating power.

params.question: A medico-legal bone-age report states: 'Skeletal maturity corresponds to exactly 16 years.' What is the most significant deficiency in this report?

answers.text: It gives a single-year estimate instead of an age range with a stated margin of error

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Bone age is an estimate of biological maturity, not a direct readout of calendar age. The report must state a range with a margin — for example, '15 to 17 years' — to reflect inherent biological and methodological variation. A single-year claim without qualification is a red flag for unsound interpretation.

answers.text: It should have reported chronological age rather than skeletal maturity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The purpose of bone-age estimation IS to assess skeletal maturity, which may differ from chronological age. The deficiency lies not in reporting skeletal maturity, but in expressing it as a single point instead of a range with a margin.

answers.text: Bone-age estimation is invalid after 14 years of age and should not have been attempted

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bone-age estimation can be performed at any age using age-appropriate methods. For older teenagers, late-fusing sites such as the medial clavicle and iliac crest provide reliable data. The error here is the point estimate, not the age of the subject.

answers.text: It is invalid because bone-age determination must rely on dental assessment alone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dental findings are a valuable corroborative tool but are not the sole basis for age estimation. Radiographic skeletal assessment is standard practice. The deficiency is the single-year figure without a stated margin of uncertainty.

overallFeedback.feedback: Bone age must always be reported as a range with a stated margin of error, never as a single exact year. A point estimate without qualification is a red flag for unsound interpretation. The report should also name the method and reference standard used.
Well done. Courts and clinicians should challenge single-year bone-age claims. A proper report names the method, names the reference standard, and states a range — never a point estimate.
